headline: A handful of healthy soil contains more organisms than people on Earth
universal_truth: The most important work often happens out of sight
fun_facts: One teaspoon of soil can contain 1 billion bacteria and miles of fungal threads
Earthworms turn over 10-15 tons of soil per acre per year—nature's plows
Dead leaves become soil through the work of billions of unseen decomposers
discussion_questions: What important work happens 'underground' in your life or organization?
Why do we rarely think about soil despite depending on it for all food?
What would happen if soil organisms stopped working?

hook.script: We walk on it without a thought. Dirt. Soil. The ground. But that brown stuff beneath your feet is the most alive place on Earth. A single handful contains more organisms than there are people on the planet. Soil isn't dead—it's teeming.

cliff.script: Every fallen leaf, every dead animal, every bit of organic matter—it all disappears into the soil. Where does it go? What invisible army breaks down everything that dies and recycles it into new life?
cliff.prompt: Who breaks down dead matter into soil?

options.text: Billions of bacteria, fungi, worms, and microorganisms working together
options.response: Yes. An invisible workforce of decomposers recycles all death into new life.

options.text: Chemical reactions break down organic matter over time
options.response: Chemistry is involved, but life does most of the work...

fact1.title: Billions Per Teaspoon
fact1.script: A single teaspoon of healthy soil contains up to 1 billion bacteria, yards of fungal threads, thousands of protozoa, and dozens of nematodes. You're standing on the most densely populated ecosystem on Earth.

fact2.title: Earth's Recyclers
fact2.script: Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up forever. Forests would be buried in their own leaves. Instead, bacteria, fungi, and invertebrates break everything down, releasing nutrients for new growth. Death feeds life feeds death—endlessly.

fact3.title: Worm Engineers
fact3.script: Earthworms are soil engineers. They eat organic matter, digest it, and excrete nutrient-rich castings. They dig tunnels that aerate soil and help water penetrate. Darwin spent years studying worms—he knew they quietly transform the world.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: The most important work often happens out of sight. The billions of soil organisms ask no recognition yet make all visible life possible. Honor the unseen work—in nature and in life.

outro.script: That's Day 66. Tomorrow, we'll discover the stories rocks tell. Until then, look at the ground differently—it's more alive than the world above it.

growTrack.title: Underground Work - Honor the Invisible
growTrack.learning_objective: Recognize and appreciate unseen essential work
growTrack.activity: Identify someone whose essential work usually goes unnoticed—maybe someone who maintains systems, cleans up, or supports behind the scenes. Thank them today. Like soil organisms, they make visible life possible.
